public_rationale: Ramp reported paid adoption spreading beyond tech before the post. That is relevant counterevidence, but adoption is not the same as substantial spending. The reviewed sources do not establish how rare substantial spending was among non-tech businesses or whether that spending was beginning to broaden. Neither concentration among large customers nor widespread inexpensive subscriptions settles the claim.
limitations: Ramp measures its own customer population.
The spending and prevalence thresholds are unspecified.
The latest monthly report available before publication covered July, not August.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Very few companies outside tech and AI are willing to pay much for AI, and there is no clear way to reverse this.
conditions: outside of the tech and AI world

statement.excerpt: In other words, outside of the tech and AI world, very few companies are willing to pay very much for AI, which is catastrophic on just about every level, with no clear sign as to how you reverse the trend.

from_speaker: outside of the tech and AI world
willing to pay very much for AI
no clear sign as to how you reverse the trend
our_interpretation: The plain reading is that substantial recurring AI spending is uncommon among non-tech businesses. Buying an inexpensive subscription alone does not contradict this.
Substantial means a meaningful business expenditure rather than experimentation or nominal subscription spending. The speaker supplies no monetary cutoff.
The reversal clause concerns signs of spending broadening at publication, not a prediction that reversal can never happen.
Use July 2026, the latest monthly spending period covered by Ramp reporting demonstrably public before the post. Ramp's August update was published September 9.
The claim concerns businesses generally. Ramp's customers are a sample, not the entire business population.
The description 'catastrophic' is an evaluative judgment and is not scored.
criteria.support_condition: Representative expenditure data show that substantial recurring AI spending was confined to a small minority of non-tech businesses, with contemporaneous evidence showing no clear broadening of substantial spending.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative expenditure data show substantial recurring AI spending was common across non-tech businesses, or a clear contemporary trend toward such spending was already visible. Adoption counts alone are insufficient.
